body_markdown:
I have always thought that round-and-round is much better than up-and-down. Before you snicker, I am talking about the rotary engine versus the reciprocating engine. I like to think I know what I’m talking about, because I owned[rotary-engined Mazda RX-7 sports cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/your-handy-1979-85-mazda-rx-7-fb-buyers-guide/) (Series 2 FB and Turbo II FC) from 1982 until 2002.


I reluctantly exchanged the Turbo II for a sensible sedan when I became a grandfather, as cautious new parents ventured that babies and sports cars didn’t mix, even though the RX-7 was equipped with ISOFIX safety latches for child seats in the rear. The sensible sedan was the luxury version of the Skoda Octavia, whose saving grace was that it boasted the same 1.8-liter turbo motor as the sporty Audi TT, although the Audi had a bit more power.


The good old FC Turbo II.


Ivan Berg


I drove almost 70,000 miles around the U.K. in the 14 years I owned the Series 2 RX-7 FB, and unusually for the rotary engine, it never let me down—not even once. Because rotary engines have a reputation for being notoriously unreliable, I can hear you asking “How is that possible?”


Well, first of all, my car was looked after by a Ferrari-trained Italian automotive engineer who happened to like the simplicity of the rotary engine and had a garage that specialized in RX-7s. Once a year, Carlo would pick up the car and give it a thorough going over. He would phone if anything more than a service needed to be done. Over time he installed some rubber boots, new suspension bushings, and, eventually, a new muffler. I never knew if he ever fitted Mazda’s latest rotor seals—he certainly never said as much—but the car always felt better to drive when after he’d returned it. The standard tires and wheels were a bit narrow, and the car was frisky when it was wet, so Carlo found an aftermarket set of wider alloys and fitted them with Pirelli Cinturatos.


Mazda


Mazda


Mazda


Second of all, I mostly respected the beep the car made when the engine revs hit 7000 rpm, even though it felt like it wanted to keep on going. Despite the RX-7’s recirculating ball steering, which nevertheless, was direct and nicely weighted, I really enjoyed driving it, and changing gear at just under 7000 rpm was a dream. The pedals were perfectly spaced for double-clutching, and I have been double-clutching since, well, since the synchromesh packed up in my Mini Cooper in 1963.


Then there’s the sound. Some have said it’s like a jet airplane. At high revs, mine howled. It had a push-in-the-back urge, and even up a long incline in third gear the car would pass everything with ease. Rarely have I felt that in other cars I have driven. I put it down to the flywheel effect of the heavy twin rotors spinning at such high revs. The engine howl perfectly complemented Dire Straits’ “Money for Nothing” playing loudly in the cassette player.


Mazda


Screaming along in third gear, I was actually giving the rotary an “Italian Tune-up,” getting it hot enough to burn off the accumulated carbon deposits in the combustion chambers, exhaust, and, most importantly, on the rotor seals. Carbon deposits are the true flaw of the rotary. Combustion is inefficient, and if the car is driven slowly, as in a city commute, carbon will build. So, if you often drive your RX-7 slowly, I’d suggest finding a long hill and giving the car an Italian Tune-up.


Of course, the “flywheel effect” doesn’t compensate for the car’s relatively low power output of around 110 horsepower and notoriously poor torque. But the car is very light, weighing just over 1,000 kg (2200 pounds), so the power-to-weight-ratio is high. I know it’s not a lot by today’s standards, but I remember the car feeling very nippy and rewarding to drive.


Ivan Berg


My most memorable and longest drive in the RX-7 came in the early morning sunshine, starting in Inverness in the Scottish Highlands, then down the picturesque east coast of Scotland, bypassing Glasgow, and on and on, and on and on, swooping downhill, howling uphill, stopping only for fuel and food and a visit to the restroom before I hit London. I feel breathless just writing about it. Google says the trip is 555 miles, with nonstop drive time listed as 10–11 hours in perfect conditions. The conditions were indeed perfect. Until I hit commuter traffic around Glasgow, anyhow. Did I knock any time off it? Probably not. But I don’t remember stopping for very long.


I only became a rotary engine enthusiast after buying and driving an RX-7. I was a fan of Citroëns, particularly the graceful and innovative DS21 Safari station wagon, which took the family to Denmark with a small sailing boat on top, and in the following year, down to the South of France.


When I walked into the Mazda showroom on that memorable day in 1982, I was intending to buy my daughter’s first car, a red Mazda 323 LX sedan. But sitting alongside it was a good looking blue sports coupe. I did the deal on the 323, but couldn’t keep my eyes off the blue car. The salesman told me it was an RX-7 and offered a test drive the next day.


Many fond memories in this Series 2 FB.


Ivan Berg


I went back the next morning with my 12-year-old son Nik ([Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/) , now Hagerty’s European Correspondent). The car was waiting for us in the loading road behind the showroom. Nik squeezed himself into one of the tiny rear +2 seats, the salesman opened the driver’s door for me, and then got in alongside. The test drive was a revelation. In comparison to the Citroën GS I had bought as a company car just the previous year, the RX-7 felt extraordinarily quick and planted. It cornered flat, unlike the leaning GS.


I was sold. Back in the showroom I asked how much would be offered for the low-mileage Citroën. The salesman said he would get back to me. He then went over to a framed poster on the wall with a side view of the RX-7 that stated: “The RX-7. Fast. But Not Furious.” He lifted it off the wall and handed it to me. “You can keep it, whether you buy the car or not,” he said. I’m looking at it now. It’s sitting on my office wall.


Berg has kept the framed poster far longer than he owned the RX-7.


Ivan Berg


Despite the very poor offer on the Citroën, I bought the Mazda. Then, 14 years later, I traded it in for what *Autocar* magazine called “Mazda’s 200 hp Supercar,” the Turbo II FC. It was white, a one-owner car, and had recently undergone a full engine rebuild with new long-lasting rotor seals. The no-lag twin scroll turbo easily took care of the rotary’s poor torque.


I only kept it six years, until 2002, for the domestic reasons named the top of this article.


Goodbye, Turbo II.


Ivan Berg


I was really sorry to see it go, as you might imagine. Even then, it was already becoming a fairly rare classic. Now, of course, low-mileage, cared-for examples like mine can fetch[close to $45,000](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mazda/rx~7/1991/1991-mazda-rx~7-turbo?id=aCn1I000000DJqUSAW) in the U.S. Meanwhile, very nice[FB Series 2 prices](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/mazda/rx-7#_) can range between $20,000 and $35,000, depending on mileage and condition.


And here, for your edification, is a list of the primary causes of rotary engine failure, which can and do happen but thankfully never happened to me…


1. Apex seal wear and breakage
2. Housing scoring caused when lubrication breaks down
3. Overheating
4. Coolant seal failure


Nevertheless, I still think that round-and-round is better than up-and-down. There has to be a way forward.


The FB Series 2 Mazda Heritage Fleet[car that Nik and I drove in 2022](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/full-circle-my-dad-revisits-the-mazda-rx-7-after-buying-one-40-years-ago/) .


Ivan Berg
